title: Why Faults Snap
question: Why do faults move in sudden jolts instead of sliding smoothly?
hook: Two sides of a fault can stay locked while the plates around them keep moving, until the stored strain lets go all at once.
idea: Rough spots lock a fault, stress builds as the plates move, and the sudden slip that breaks through releases the stored energy as an earthquake.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of an earthquake on a fault in order.
items: Moving plates build stress and stored strain
Stress breaks through and the fault slides
Stored energy leaves as waves, heat and cracking
beats.explain: Locking comes first, strain builds while the plates keep moving, the rough spot gives way, and only then is the energy released.

beats.prompt: A fault's two faces have no rough spots at all. What happens as the plates move?

choices.label: Huge quakes, since nothing slows the sides
choices.feedback: Nothing slows them, which is exactly why no strain gets stored up for a big release.

choices.label: The sides slide past smoothly and quietly
The sides cannot move at all
choices.feedback: Smooth faces add no extra friction, so the sides are free to move.

beats.explain: Without rough spots adding friction, the sides of a fault move past each other smoothly and without earthquakes.

beats.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Ground point straight above the rupture start
Frequency, type and size of quakes over time
Average seismic energy released per unit volume
beats.explain: Two terms place a quake in space, and two describe how active an area is.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: An earthquake releases strain energy stored around a fault.
Only about 10 percent or less leaves as seismic waves.
So the shaking carries most of the quake's energy.
The rest powers fracture growth or becomes frictional heat.
beats.explain: If seismic waves take 10 percent or less, most of the energy goes elsewhere, into breaking rock and heat.
